docs.title: Why MCP, and why now
docs.text:
By late 2026 almost every serious AI agent — in an IDE, a desktop app, a backend service — talks to its tools and data through the same open protocol instead of a different bespoke integration for every provider. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes that connection: a host application runs a client, the client speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 to one or more servers, and each server exposes tools, resources and prompts in a predictable, inspectable way. That's the same mechanism powering the tool access this very assistant uses.

This course treats MCP as its own discipline: the wire protocol underneath it, how to build and ship a real server in Python or TypeScript, how to run several servers together reliably and securely, and how to operate MCP infrastructure at production scale — not just wire up one example and call it done.

docs.title: 01 · What Is MCP & Why It Exists
The problem: every app, every tool, a bespoke integration
docs.text:
Say you're building an AI assistant that needs to read a user's calendar and post messages to Slack. Without a shared protocol, you write:

  • A calendar integration specific to your assistant's internals
  • A Slack integration specific to your assistant's internals

Now say a second assistant wants the same two capabilities. It writes its own calendar integration and its own Slack integration — different code, different auth handling, different error conventions, even though the underlying capability ("read events", "post a message") is identical.

With M AI applications and N tools/data sources, you end up writing roughly M × N integrations. Every new assistant re-implements every integration. Every new tool has to be wired into every assistant that wants to use it.

docs.title: The fix: a shared protocol in the middle
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines a standard way for an AI application to discover and call tools, read data, and use prompt templates — regardless of which AI application it is, and regardless of which tool or data source is on the other end.

With MCP, the calendar integration is written once, as an MCP server. Any MCP-compatible AI application can connect to it and immediately get calendar tools, with no calendar-specific code in the application itself. The Slack integration is written once too. The math changes from M × N to M + N: M applications each implement the client side of MCP once, N tools each implement the server side of MCP once, and any client can talk to any server.

Without MCP (M × N):              With MCP (M + N):

Assistant A ─── Calendar          Assistant A ─┐
Assistant A ─── Slack                          ├── MCP ──── Calendar Server
Assistant B ─── Calendar          Assistant B ─┘        └── Slack Server
Assistant B ─── Slack

docs.title: Why this will look familiar: the Language Server Protocol
docs.text:
MCP was directly inspired by the Language Server Protocol (LSP), which solved the exact same shape of problem for code editors. Before LSP, every editor (VS Code, Vim, Emacs, Sublime...) had to implement its own autocomplete, go-to-definition, and linting support for every programming language it wanted to support well — again, an M × N problem.

LSP fixed it: a language's tooling author writes one language server (for Python, for Rust, for Go...). Any LSP-compatible editor can talk to any language server over the same protocol. Your editor doesn't need to know anything about Rust's compiler internals — it just needs to speak LSP, and the Rust language server handles the rest.

MCP applies the same idea to AI applications and the tools/data they need: write the tool integration once, as an MCP server, and every MCP-compatible AI application — Claude Desktop, an IDE, a custom agent — can use it without custom code.

docs.title: A concrete example
docs.text:
Imagine an MCP server that exposes two tools against a calendar API: list_events(start_date, end_date) and create_event(title, start, end), and a separate MCP server that exposes post_message(channel, text) against Slack's API.

An AI assistant connected to both servers can be asked, in plain language, "Check my calendar for conflicts tomorrow afternoon and post a summary to

docs.title: team-standup" — and it will call list_events, reason about the results,
docs.text:
then call post_message, without the assistant's own codebase containing a single line of calendar-specific or Slack-specific code. All of that logic lives in the two servers, where it was written once.

This course builds exactly that kind of server, starting from scratch, over the next 40 lessons — level 1 gets you to a real, working local server by lesson 10.

docs.title: 02 · JSON-RPC 2.0: The Wire Protocol Underneath
docs.text: MCP doesn't invent its own wire format. Every message that flows between an MCP client and an MCP server is a JSON-RPC 2.0 message — a small, well established spec for calling methods and getting results back as JSON. Understanding JSON-RPC directly demystifies everything MCP does later: tool calls, resource reads, prompt fetches, even the connection handshake are all just JSON-RPC requests and responses with MCP-specific method names and payloads.

docs.title: The three message shapes
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 has exactly three kinds of messages.

A request — asks the other side to do something and expects a reply:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "add",
    "arguments": { "a": 2, "b": 3 }
  }
}

A response — the reply to a request, matched by id, with either a result or an error, never both:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "5" }]
  }
}

A notification — a one-way message with no id and no reply expected:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "method": "notifications/initialized",
  "params": {}
}

That's the entire vocabulary. method is always a string naming the operation. params carries whatever arguments that operation needs. id is how a response gets matched back to the request that triggered it — present on requests and their responses, absent on notifications.

docs.title: Core MCP methods, in JSON-RPC terms
docs.text:
Every MCP operation you'll learn in this course is one of these shapes with a specific method name:

MCP operation method Request or notification? Open a connection initialize Request Confirm the connection is ready notifications/initialized Notification List available tools tools/list Request Call a tool tools/call Request List available resources resources/list Request Read a resource resources/read Request List available prompts prompts/list Request Get a prompt prompts/get Request

You'll meet initialize and the three */list + */call-or-/read-or-/get pairs properly in the next two lessons. For now, just notice: they're all plain JSON-RPC requests with an MCP-specific method string.

docs.title: A full exchange over stdio
docs.text:
Here's what actually crosses the wire for a single tool call, assuming the connection is already initialized. Each JSON-RPC message is sent as one line of JSON, terminated by a newline — this matters later when you build a server, because printing anything else to stdout will break this framing.

Client sends (asking what tools exist):

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}

Server replies:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"tools":[{"name":"add","description":"Add two numbers","inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"integer"},"b":{"type":"integer"}},"required":["a","b"]}}]}}

Client sends (actually calling it):

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"add","arguments":{"a":2,"b":3}}}

Server replies:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"result":{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"5"}]}}

Four messages, two request/response pairs, matched by id. Nothing more exotic is happening underneath any MCP tool call you'll make in this course.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. A missing id is the entire signal for "notification." There's no separate type field distinguishing a request from a notification — the spec says: if id is present, it's a request and a response is required; if id is absent, it's a notification and the receiver must not reply. notifications/initialized is a notification precisely because the client doesn't need (and the server must not send) a response to it.

  2. id can be a number or a string, and the sender chooses it — it just has to be unique among that sender's currently-outstanding requests so responses can be matched back correctly. Most SDKs auto-increment an integer counter for you.

  3. Errors are a specific object shape, not just any JSON. A JSON-RPC error response looks like: 

    {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"Invalid params"}}
    code is a signed integer (the JSON-RPC spec reserves a range of negative codes for protocol-level errors like "method not found" or "invalid params"; MCP and application code can define their own codes outside that reserved range for domain-specific failures), and message is a short human-readable string. An optional data field can carry additional structured detail.

  4. Batching exists in the JSON-RPC 2.0 spec (sending an array of requests in one message) but MCP does not use it — every MCP message is sent as a single JSON object per line, never an array.

docs.title: 03 · MCP Architecture: Hosts, Clients & Servers
docs.text: MCP defines three distinct roles. Getting these precise — especially the one-to-one rule below — makes everything else in this course easier to reason about.

docs.title: The three roles
docs.text:
Host — the AI application the user actually interacts with: Claude Desktop, an IDE with AI features, a custom agent application. The host is responsible for managing the overall conversation, enforcing permissions, and deciding which servers to connect to.

Client — lives inside the host, and manages the connection to exactly one server. If a host wants to use three different MCP servers, it creates and owns three separate client instances internally — one per server. This is a strict 1:1 relationship: a single client never multiplexes connections to more than one server.

Server — a (usually small, often standalone) program that exposes capabilities — tools, resources, prompts — to whichever client connects to it. A server doesn't know or care which host it's ultimately serving; it just speaks MCP to its one connected client.

┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Host (e.g. Claude Desktop)           │
│                                      │
│   ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐           │
│   │Client A│   │Client B│           │
│   └───┬────┘   └───┬────┘           │
└───────┼────────────┼────────────────┘
        │ 1:1         │ 1:1
        ▼             ▼
   Server A      Server B
  (calendar)       (Slack)

Note what this diagram rules out: Client A never talks to Server B. If the host wants to use both the calendar and Slack servers, it runs two clients, each wired to exactly one server.

docs.title: Capabilities, not a fixed feature set
docs.text: A server doesn't have to expose tools, resources, and prompts — it declares which of these it actually implements. This declaration happens during the initialize handshake (next section), so the client knows upfront what it can ask for and never has to guess or trial-and-error its way into discovering what a server supports.

docs.title: Server-side vs. client-side primitives
docs.text:
The three primitives you'll spend most of this level on are all things a server offers:

Primitive What it is Who controls when it's used Tools Functions the model can call to take an action The model decides, based on the user's request Resources Data the client can read (files, records, docs) The application or user typically selects these Prompts Reusable, parameterized prompt templates The user typically invokes these explicitly

MCP also defines two primitives that flow the other direction — a client-side capability a server can request:

Primitive What it is Sampling A server can ask the client to run an LLM completion on its behalf, without the server needing its own API key or model access Roots A client can tell a server which filesystem directories (or other URI scopes) it's allowed to operate within

You'll build and use tools, resources, and prompts throughout this level. Sampling and roots are proper, hands-on topics in Level 2 and Level 3 — for now, just know they exist and which direction they flow.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The connection between a client and a server goes through a fixed lifecycle every single time, regardless of transport:

  1. Transport connects. For a local server this means the host spawns your server as a subprocess and opens its stdin/stdout; for a remote server it means an HTTP connection is established. Either way, no MCP messages have been exchanged yet — just a raw channel.
  2. initialize request. The client sends an initialize request containing its own protocol version and the capabilities it supports (e.g. whether it can handle sampling requests).
  3. initialize response. The server replies with its protocol version and the capabilities it supports — which of tools, resources, and prompts it actually implements, plus any optional features within each.
  4. notifications/initialized. The client sends this one-way notification confirming it received and accepted the server's capabilities. Only after this point is the connection considered fully open.
  5. Normal operation. Only now will the client send tools/list, resources/read, and so on. A server that receives one of these before the handshake completes is within its rights to reject it.

This matters practically: the SDK you'll use in the next lesson handles this handshake for you automatically, but when something is silently not working later in this course — a tool doesn't show up, a resource read hangs — the first thing worth checking is whether the handshake actually completed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
For each of these three scenarios, write one sentence identifying which primitive (tool, resource, or prompt) fits best, and why:

  1. An assistant needs to read the contents of README.md in the user's project so it can answer a question about the project.
  2. A user wants a one-click way to generate a standardized "weekly status update" write-up, filling in a project name and a list of accomplishments.
  3. An assistant needs to create a new GitHub issue based on a bug the user just described.

docs.title: 04 · Setup: Python SDK & Your First Server
Install the SDK
docs.text:
The official Python SDK is published as the mcp package, and it ships the FastMCP helper class that this entire course uses to build servers.

pip install mcp

You'll also want the MCP Inspector, a browser-based tool for poking at a server interactively without needing a full host application like Claude Desktop. It's a Node package, run directly with npx (no install needed):

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

Keep that command handy — you'll use it in a moment.

docs.title: Your first server
docs.text:
Create server.py:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("demo-server")

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers together."""
    return a + b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

That's a complete, working MCP server. FastMCP("demo-server") creates a server named demo-server. The @mcp.tool() decorator registers add as a tool the server exposes. mcp.run() starts the server, defaulting to the stdio transport covered in lesson 8 — it blocks and waits for a client to connect over stdin/stdout.

Run it directly and it'll just sit there, waiting:

python server.py

That's expected — a stdio server has nothing to say until a client connects to it. Press Ctrl+C to stop it; you'll connect to it properly next.

docs.title: Inspecting it
docs.text:
The MCP Inspector gives you a client to talk to your server without writing one yourself. Run:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py

This opens a browser UI. The Inspector launches your server.py as a subprocess (the same way a real host application would), connects to it, and lets you:

  • See the initialize handshake and the capabilities your server reported
  • Browse the tools/list response — you should see add listed, with a JSON Schema generated from its type hints
  • Call add with real arguments and see the tools/call request and response, exactly as described in lesson 2

Try calling add with a=2, b=3 and confirm you get 5 back, then watch the raw JSON-RPC messages in the Inspector's message log — it's the fastest way to connect everything from the last three lessons to something real.

docs.text: Add a second tool to server.py called multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int that returns the product. Restart the Inspector, confirm both add and multiply appear in tools/list, and call multiply with two different pairs of numbers to confirm it works.

docs.title: 05 · Tools: Exposing Functions to an LLM
docs.text: A tool is an action the model can decide to take — look something up, change something, compute something. Lesson 4 already showed the basic shape; this lesson goes one level deeper into how a plain function becomes a tool the model can actually use well.

docs.title: Type hints become the schema
docs.text:
Recall tools/list returns an inputSchema — a JSON Schema describing what arguments a tool accepts. With FastMCP, you never write that schema by hand. It's generated directly from your function's type hints:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("demo-server")

@mcp.tool()
def convert_currency(amount: float, from_currency: str, to_currency: str) -> str:
    """Convert an amount from one currency to another using a fixed demo rate."""
    rates = {"USD": 1.0, "EUR": 0.92, "GBP": 0.79}
    if from_currency not in rates or to_currency not in rates:
        return f"Unsupported currency: must be one of {list(rates)}"
    usd = amount / rates[from_currency]
    converted = usd * rates[to_currency]
    return f"{amount} {from_currency} = {converted:.2f} {to_currency}"

amount: float, from_currency: str, and to_currency: str become three required properties in the generated inputSchema, typed number and string respectively. There's no separate schema file or decorator argument to keep in sync — the signature is the source of truth.

docs.title: The docstring is what the model reads
docs.text:
The model doesn't see your Python source code. What it sees, via tools/list, is the tool's name, its description (taken from the docstring), and its inputSchema. A vague docstring produces a tool the model will use incorrectly or not at all; a precise one does the opposite. Compare:

@mcp.tool()
def search(q: str) -> str:
    """Search."""  # the model has almost nothing to go on
    ...

@mcp.tool()
def search_orders(customer_email: str) -> str:
    """Look up all orders placed by a customer, given their email address.
    Returns order IDs, dates, and statuses."""
    ...

The second version tells the model exactly when to reach for this tool and what it will get back — that description is doing real work.

docs.title: Multiple tools, one server
docs.text:
A single server can expose as many tools as make sense for the thing it wraps. Each one just needs its own @mcp.tool()-decorated function:

@mcp.tool()
def list_orders(customer_email: str) -> str:
    """List all orders for a customer."""
    ...

@mcp.tool()
def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Get the current status of a single order by its ID."""
    ...

@mcp.tool()
def cancel_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Cancel an order by its ID, if it hasn't shipped yet."""
    ...

Each tool gets its own name, description, and schema in tools/list — the model picks whichever one fits the user's request.

docs.title: Returning structured data
docs.text:
Everything so far returns a plain string, which becomes a single {"type": "text", "text": "..."} content block in the tools/call response. You can also return a list or dict of JSON-serializable data, and FastMCP will serialize it for you — useful when the result has real structure the model should reason over, like a list of order records rather than a hand-formatted sentence:

@mcp.tool()
def list_orders(customer_email: str) -> list[dict]:
    """List all orders for a customer as structured records."""
    return [
        {"order_id": "A1", "status": "shipped", "total": 42.50},
        {"order_id": "A2", "status": "processing", "total": 19.99},
    ]

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a tool word_count(text: str) -> dict that returns a dictionary with three keys: "characters" (total character count), "words" (count of whitespace-separated tokens), and "lines" (count of newline-separated lines). Give it a docstring precise enough that a model would know exactly when to call it, then verify it in the Inspector with a short multi-line string.

docs.title: 06 · Resources: Exposing Data to an LLM
Resources vs. tools: the real distinction
docs.text:
It's tempting to think "a resource is just a tool that returns data," but the distinction that actually matters is about control, not shape:

  • A tool is called when the model decides, mid-conversation, that calling it will help answer the user. The model chooses the arguments.
  • A resource is typically read because the application or user explicitly attached it — picked a file from a list, pasted a link, or the host proactively loaded it as context before the conversation even reaches the model.

A file's contents, a database record, a config value — things that are simply there to be read, with no side effects and no decision-making required — are resources. An action that changes something, searches with arbitrary model-chosen parameters, or has side effects belongs as a tool.

docs.title: Exposing a resource
docs.text:
The @mcp.resource() decorator takes a URI and registers a function to handle it. This lesson covers static URIs — fixed, exact strings. Templated URIs with variable segments (notes://{note_id}, for example) are a Level 2 topic, once you've got the fixed case solid.

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("demo-server")

@mcp.resource("config://app-settings")
def get_app_settings() -> str:
    """The current application settings, as JSON."""
    return '{"theme": "dark", "notifications": true}'

The URI's scheme (config:// here) is entirely up to you — MCP doesn't mandate a fixed set of schemes. Pick something that describes what the resource actually is: file://, config://, notes://, whatever reads clearly for your server.

docs.title: Multiple resources
docs.text:
Just like tools, a server can expose as many resources as it needs:

@mcp.resource("docs://readme")
def get_readme() -> str:
    """The project's README file."""
    with open("README.md") as f:
        return f.read()

@mcp.resource("docs://changelog")
def get_changelog() -> str:
    """The project's changelog."""
    with open("CHANGELOG.md") as f:
        return f.read()

A client calling resources/list gets back both URIs with their descriptions, and can then resources/read whichever one it actually needs — mirroring the tools/list → tools/call pattern from lesson 5, but for reading instead of acting.

docs.title: When you genuinely need both
docs.text:
Nothing stops a server from offering a resource and a tool that overlap in subject matter, as long as each is doing the job it's suited for:

@mcp.resource("orders://all")
def all_orders() -> list[dict]:
    """The full current order list, as structured records."""
    return load_all_orders()

@mcp.tool()
def search_orders(status: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Search orders by status (e.g. 'shipped', 'pending')."""
    return [o for o in load_all_orders() if o["status"] == status]

The resource is the whole dataset, available for a client to load as context whenever it wants. The tool is a model-driven, parameterized query against that same data — the model decides what status to search for based on what the user actually asked.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a resource stats://summary to a server of your own that returns a short string summarizing some data you already have lying around (a word count of a file, the number of lines in a log, anything). Confirm in the Inspector that it shows up under resources/list and that reading it returns the right content.

docs.title: What a prompt template actually is
docs.text:
A prompt in MCP is a reusable, parameterized piece of prompt text that a server offers — think of it as a saved, fill-in-the-blanks request. Where a tool is something the model decides to call mid-conversation, a prompt is something the user typically invokes explicitly, the way you'd pick a saved template from a menu rather than describe what you want from scratch every time.

Hosts commonly surface prompts as quick-actions or slash-commands in their UI — the user sees a list of available prompts by name and picks one, rather than the model silently choosing to use one.

docs.title: Defining a prompt
docs.text:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("demo-server")

@mcp.prompt()
def code_review(language: str, focus: str = "general code quality") -> str:
    """Generate a code review request for a given language and focus area."""
    return (
        f"Please review the following {language} code, focusing on "
        f"{focus}. Point out specific issues with line references, and "
        f"suggest concrete fixes rather than general advice."
    )

@mcp.prompt() works the same way @mcp.tool() does: the function's type hints become the prompt's argument schema, and the docstring becomes its description. language is required (no default), focus is optional (it has a default value). A client calling prompts/get with {"language": "Python"} gets back the fully-rendered prompt text with focus filled in from its default.

docs.title: Arguments with defaults vs. without
docs.text:
@mcp.prompt()
def summarize(text: str, max_sentences: int = 3) -> str:
    """Summarize a block of text in a target number of sentences."""
    return f"Summarize the following text in at most {max_sentences} sentences:\n\n{text}"

Here text must be supplied every time; max_sentences falls back to 3 when the caller doesn't specify it. This is exactly how optional tool arguments behave too — the same Python defaults mechanism drives both.

docs.title: Prompt or tool — which one?
docs.text:
Ask: is this something the user explicitly chooses to trigger, with a roughly fixed shape each time ("review this code," "summarize this text," "write a commit message for this diff")? That's a prompt. Is it something the model should decide to reach for on its own, based on reasoning about what the user's actual request needs? That's a tool.

A "generate a weekly status report" request the user runs the same way every Friday is a good prompt — it's a known, repeatable shape of request. A "look up this customer's order history" request that the model should trigger automatically whenever it's relevant to the conversation is a tool — the model needs to decide when it applies, not the user.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a prompt explain_error(error_message: str, language: str = "Python") that returns a request asking for a plain-English explanation of the given error message and, if applicable, a likely fix, in the context of the given language. Confirm in the Inspector that prompts/get with just an error_message argument still works correctly, falling back to the language default.

docs.title: How stdio transport actually works
docs.text:
When a host connects to a local MCP server, it doesn't open a network socket — it spawns your server as a subprocess and talks to it over that process's standard input and standard output. This is the stdio transport, and it's what mcp.run() defaults to when you don't specify anything else.

Concretely: the host runs something equivalent to subprocess.Popen(["python", "server.py"], stdin=PIPE, stdout=PIPE). Every JSON-RPC message the host sends gets written to your server's stdin, one JSON object per line, newline-terminated. Every message your server sends back gets written to stdout in the same format. There's no HTTP, no sockets, no ports to configure — just a pipe in each direction.

This is why stdio is the default and simplest choice for local servers: there's effectively zero setup beyond "run this command," which is exactly what you'll register in claude_desktop_config.json in the next lesson.

docs.title: The one rule you cannot break
docs.text:
Because stdout is the literal protocol channel, anything your server prints to stdout other than well-formed JSON-RPC messages corrupts the stream and breaks the connection — often in confusing ways, since the failure shows up as a parse error on whichever message happened to follow the stray output.

This means a plain print() call anywhere in your server's code, including deep inside a library you're calling, is a real bug:

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    print(f"Adding {a} and {b}")  # BUG: this corrupts the stdio stream
    return a + b

That innocent-looking debug print() writes Adding 2 and 3 straight into the same stream the client is trying to parse as JSON-RPC. The client will fail to parse it, and depending on timing, may also fail to parse the next legitimate message because the stream is now out of sync.

docs.title: Log to stderr instead
docs.text:
Standard error is a separate stream, untouched by the protocol — it's the right place for anything you want to see while debugging, and FastMCP servers can write there freely:

import sys

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    print(f"Adding {a} and {b}", file=sys.stderr)  # safe
    return a + b

Or, more idiomatically, use Python's logging module configured to a stream handler on stderr (the standard library default for logging.StreamHandler() with no argument), which gives you levels and formatting for free without any risk of touching stdout.

docs.title: Why this doesn't apply equally to every transport
docs.text: This specific gotcha is unique to stdio. Lesson 2 of Level 2 covers Streamable HTTP transport, where the protocol messages travel over HTTP request/response bodies instead of a shared process stream — ordinary console output there doesn't collide with anything. But stdio is what every local server you build in this level uses, so the habit of never touching stdout starts now.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take the server.py from lesson 4 and deliberately add a print() statement inside the add tool, pointed at stdout. Run it through the MCP Inspector and call add — observe what actually happens (a parse error, a hang, or a garbled response, depending on your SDK version and timing). Then fix it by redirecting that same debug line to sys.stderr and confirm the tool call works cleanly again.

docs.title: 09 · Connecting Your Server to Claude Desktop
docs.text: Everything so far has run through the MCP Inspector. This lesson connects the same server to a real host application — Claude Desktop — so you can use it in an actual conversation.

docs.title: The config file
docs.text:
Claude Desktop reads its MCP server list from a JSON config file, claude_desktop_config.json, located at:

  • macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json
  • Linux: ~/.config/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json

If the file doesn't exist yet, create it. The relevant shape is an mcpServers object, where each key is a name you choose for the server and each value describes how to launch it:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "demo-server": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/server.py"]
    }
  }
}

command is the executable to run, args is the list of arguments passed to it — together they're exactly the subprocess invocation Claude Desktop will spawn, the same way the Inspector spawned python server.py in lesson 4. Use an absolute path to server.py; Claude Desktop doesn't necessarily launch the process from the directory you expect.

docs.title: Environment variables, if your server needs them
docs.text:
If your server reads an API key or other config from the environment, add an env object alongside command and args:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "demo-server": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/server.py"],
      "env": {
        "SOME_API_KEY": "your-key-here"
      }
    }
  }
}

Your server doesn't need any special code to read this — it's set on the subprocess's environment exactly like any other environment variable, so plain os.environ["SOME_API_KEY"] in your server picks it up.

docs.title: Restart and verify
docs.text:
Config changes aren't picked up live — fully quit and reopen Claude Desktop (not just close the window) for it to re-read the file and spawn your server. If the config is valid and the server starts cleanly, you'll see a small tools/MCP indicator in the Claude Desktop UI; clicking it should list demo-server and its tools.

If it doesn't show up, check Claude Desktop's MCP log file (also under the same per-OS config directory, typically named something like mcp-server-demo-server.log) — this captures anything your server wrote to stderr plus any startup failures, and is almost always where the actual error message is.

docs.title: Use it for real
docs.text: Open a new conversation and ask something that requires the tool you built, for example, if you still have the add tool from lesson 4: "What's 47 plus 128? Use the add tool." Claude Desktop's host will present your tool to the model, the model will issue a tools/call exactly as you saw in the Inspector, and you'll get a real answer computed by your own code running on your own machine — not by the model doing arithmetic itself.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Register the notes/tasks server you'll build in lesson 10's project ahead of time by adding a second entry to mcpServers right now, pointing at a notes_server.py path that doesn't exist yet. Confirm Claude Desktop reports a startup failure for that entry in its log (rather than silently ignoring it) — this is exactly the error you'll want to recognize once you've actually built that server and are debugging why it isn't showing up.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Local Notes/Tasks MCP Server
docs.text: This project pulls together everything from Level 1: tools, a resource, and a real connection to Claude Desktop, applied to a small but genuinely useful server — a notes/tasks manager backed by a local JSON file.

docs.title: Spec
docs.text:
Build a server named notes-server with these three tools and one resource:

add_note(text: str) -> dict Adds a new note with the given text. Generates a unique ID (an incrementing integer is fine), stores it as not-yet-complete, and returns the full note record as a dict: {"id": ..., "text": ..., "done": False}.

list_notes(include_done: bool = True) -> list[dict] Returns all stored notes as a list of records. When include_done=False, filters out notes already marked done.

complete_note(note_id: int) -> dict Marks the note with the given ID as done ("done": True) and returns the updated record. If no note with that ID exists, return a dict like {"error": f"No note with id {note_id}"} instead of raising — tool results should communicate failure as data the model can read and relay, not as an unhandled exception.

Resource notes://all Returns all notes rendered as a single markdown document — one line per note, something like:

- [ ] Buy groceries (#1)
- [x] Call the dentist (#2)

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Notes must survive a server restart, so store them in a JSON file on disk (e.g. notes.json next to your server script) rather than only in memory. A reasonable structure:

import json
from pathlib import Path

NOTES_FILE = Path(__file__).parent / "notes.json"

def load_notes() -> list[dict]:
    if not NOTES_FILE.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(NOTES_FILE.read_text())

def save_notes(notes: list[dict]) -> None:
    NOTES_FILE.write_text(json.dumps(notes, indent=2))

Each tool should load the current notes, make its change, save, and return the relevant result — you decide the exact shape of load_notes / save_notes and how add_note picks the next ID (the highest existing ID plus one is a reasonable approach, since IDs may not always start at 1 after notes get removed in a future version of this server).

docs.title: Build it
docs.text: Scaffold the server the same way as lesson 4, with the three @mcp.tool()-decorated functions and one @mcp.resource("notes://all") function described above, wired to the persistence functions. The core server setup (FastMCP("notes-server"), the if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run() block) is exactly what you've already built twice this level — reuse it rather than re-deriving it.

docs.title: Verify it end to end
docs.text:
1. In the MCP Inspector, call add_note two or three times with different text, then list_notes() and confirm all of them come back.
  2. Call complete_note on one of the IDs, then list_notes(include_done=False) and confirm the completed one is filtered out while it still shows up with include_done=True.
  3. Read the notes://all resource and confirm the markdown checklist format matches what you'd expect from the current state.
  4. Restart the Inspector (which restarts your server process) and confirm list_notes() still returns the same notes — proving the JSON file persistence actually works, not just the in-memory state of a single run.
  5. Register it in claude_desktop_config.json per lesson 9, restart Claude Desktop, and ask it to add a note and then list your notes, in a real conversation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Extend the server with a fourth tool, delete_note(note_id: int) -> dict, that removes a note entirely (not just marks it done) and returns either the removed record or an error dict if the ID doesn't exist — matching the same not-found-as-data convention complete_note uses. Confirm it works in the Inspector, including the case of deleting an ID that was never added.

docs.title: Level 2 · Intermediate Production Servers
docs.text: Goal: move past a local stdio server and build something you could actually ship — remote transport, real authentication, and a server that wraps a real external API.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. The TypeScript SDK
  2. Streamable HTTP & SSE Transport

By the end of this level you'll be fluent in both the Python and TypeScript SDKs, comfortable with remote transport and OAuth 2.1, and you'll have built and deployed a real server that wraps a live external API.

docs.title: 01 · The TypeScript SDK
docs.text: Everything you built in Level 1 used Python's FastMCP. Most of the MCP ecosystem — editor extensions, Node-based backends, anything that's already a TypeScript codebase — uses the official TypeScript SDK instead. The concepts are identical: tools, resources, prompts, a transport connecting a server to a client. Only the syntax changes.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
mkdir mcp-ts-demo && cd mcp-ts-demo
npm init -y
npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod
npm install -D typescript @types/node tsx
npx tsc --init --target es2022 --module nodenext --moduleResolution nodenext

zod is a schema library the SDK uses to describe tool input shapes — it plays the same role Python's type hints played with FastMCP.

docs.title: A minimal server
docs.text:
// server.ts
import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";
import { z } from "zod";

const server = new McpServer({
  name: "ts-demo",
  version: "1.0.0",
});

server.registerTool(
  "add",
  {
    title: "Add two numbers",
    description: "Returns the sum of a and b.",
    inputSchema: { a: z.number(), b: z.number() },
  },
  async ({ a, b }) => ({
    content: [{ type: "text", text: String(a + b) }],
  })
);

const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
await server.connect(transport);

Run it with the Inspector, same as in Level 1:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector npx tsx server.ts

Compare this to Python's FastMCP:

@mcp.tool()
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Returns the sum of a and b."""
    return a + b

Python's version infers the schema from type hints and the return value is just a Python value. TypeScript's version is more explicit — you pass the schema and build the content array yourself — but the protocol-level behavior (what goes over stdio, what tools/list returns, how tools/call is dispatched) is byte-for-byte the same. A client talking to either server can't tell which language it's written in.

docs.title: A small two-tool server
docs.text:
Let's rebuild the spirit of Level 1's notes server, scaled down to two tools, to see a server with real state:

// notes-server.ts
import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js";
import { z } from "zod";

interface Note {
  id: number;
  text: string;
}

const notes: Note[] = [];
let nextId = 1;

const server = new McpServer({ name: "notes-ts", version: "1.0.0" });

server.registerTool(
  "add_note",
  {
    title: "Add a note",
    description: "Stores a new note and returns its id.",
    inputSchema: { text: z.string() },
  },
  async ({ text }) => {
    const note = { id: nextId++, text };
    notes.push(note);
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `Added note #${note.id}` }] };
  }
);

server.registerTool(
  "list_notes",
  {
    title: "List notes",
    description: "Returns every stored note.",
    inputSchema: {},
  },
  async () => ({
    content: [
      {
        type: "text",
        text: notes.map((n) => `#${n.id}: ${n.text}`).join("\n") || "(no notes yet)",
      },
    ],
  })
);

const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
await server.connect(transport);

The notes array lives in the server process's memory for as long as the process runs — the same lifetime model as the Python version from Level 1.

docs.title: When a team picks TypeScript over Python
docs.text:
• The rest of the codebase is already Node/TypeScript. A server that shares types, utilities, or an existing API client with a Next.js or Express app is simpler to keep in the same language.
  • The server needs to run in environments where Node is the standard runtime — serverless functions on platforms built around JavaScript, edge runtimes, browser-adjacent tooling.
  • Python wins when the server's real job is calling into a Python-only ecosystem — data science libraries, ML model code, anything built on pandas/NumPy/PyTorch. Wrapping that from TypeScript would mean shelling out to a Python subprocess anyway, which defeats the point.

Neither SDK is "more official" — both are maintained by Anthropic as first-class implementations of the same spec. Pick based on what the rest of your system already looks like.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third tool, complete_note, that takes a note id (number) and removes it from the notes array, returning a confirmation message — or an error message if no note with that id exists. Test it with the Inspector: add two notes, complete one, then list notes and confirm only the other one remains.

docs.title: 02 · Streamable HTTP & SSE Transport
docs.text: Everything so far has used stdio: the host spawns your server as a child process and talks to it over stdin/stdout. That only works when client and server live on the same machine. A server deployed to the cloud, shared by many users, needs a transport that works over a network — that's Streamable HTTP.

docs.title: Why stdio can't cross a network
docs.text:
stdio transport assumes:

  • The server is a subprocess the host directly spawned and owns.
  • There's exactly one client talking to exactly one server process.
  • The pipe is private — no other process can read or write it.

None of that holds for a server running on infrastructure you don't control from the client's machine. You need a transport built on a protocol that networks actually support, with a notion of separate client connections and message framing that survives going through load balancers and proxies. HTTP is that protocol.

docs.title: How Streamable HTTP works
docs.text:
A Streamable HTTP MCP server exposes a single endpoint, typically /mcp, that handles two kinds of traffic:

  • POST /mcp — the client sends a JSON-RPC request or notification as the request body. For a simple request/response exchange, the server's HTTP response body is just the JSON-RPC response.
  • GET /mcp with Accept: text/event-stream — opens a long-lived Server-Sent Events stream the server can use to push messages to the client without the client having to poll (notifications, or responses to requests the server is still processing).

A Mcp-Session-Id header, set by the server on its first response and echoed back by the client on every subsequent request, ties a sequence of HTTP requests together into one logical MCP session — the network equivalent of "the same stdio pipe."

docs.title: A minimal HTTP server (Python)
docs.text:
pip install "mcp[cli]"

# http_server.py
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("http-demo")

@mcp.tool()
def echo(message: str) -> str:
    """Returns the message back unchanged."""
    return message

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")

python http_server.py
# serving on http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp by default

Point the Inspector at a URL instead of a local command to connect to it:

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector
# then choose "Streamable HTTP" and enter http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp

docs.title: A raw POST, to see the shape
docs.text:
You don't need the Inspector to talk to this server — it's just HTTP:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{
    "jsonrpc": "2.0",
    "id": 1,
    "method": "tools/call",
    "params": {"name": "echo", "arguments": {"message": "hi"}}
  }'

The response is the same JSON-RPC result object you'd see over stdio — the transport changed, the protocol on top of it didn't.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. Every request is still JSON-RPC. Streamable HTTP doesn't change what a request, response, or notification looks like — only how the bytes get from client to server and back. tools/call over HTTP has the exact same params shape as tools/call over stdio.
  2. The session ID is the glue. stdio gets "this is the same conversation" for free, because it's one process talking over one pipe. HTTP requests are independent by default, so the server issues a Mcp-Session-Id on the initialize response, and the client must send it back on every later request so the server can find the right in-memory session state.
  3. SSE is for the server-initiated direction. A plain HTTP response can only answer the request that triggered it. But MCP needs the server to be able to send unsolicited messages — a progress notification during a long tool call, or a sampling/createMessage request asking the client's LLM for a completion. The GET endpoint's event stream is how those reach the client without the client polling.
  4. A POST can itself open a stream. If handling a request will take a while or needs to emit intermediate notifications, the server can respond to that POST with Content-Type: text/event-stream instead of a single JSON body, streaming the eventual result as one of the events.
  5. Statelessness is a deployment choice, not a protocol requirement. A server can be written to keep no session state at all (treating every request independently) specifically so it scales horizontally without sticky sessions — more on this trade-off in Level 4.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second tool to http_server.py, slow_count(n: int), that sleeps for one second n times. Run the server, then use the Inspector's "History" or network panel to watch what happens on the connection while a call to slow_count(3) is in flight — note that the HTTP request doesn't return until the tool finishes, even though nothing is streamed back incrementally in this simple version. That gap is exactly what Level 3's progress notifications are for.

docs.title: 03 · Authentication & OAuth 2.1 for Remote Servers
docs.text: A stdio server never asked you for a password, and that wasn't an oversight. A remote server can't get away with that — it needs a real authorization story. MCP specifies one, built on OAuth 2.1.

docs.title: Why stdio servers skip this entirely
docs.text:
When Claude Desktop launches your server as a subprocess, the trust decision already happened: you, the user, put that server's command in your claude_desktop_config.json. The server only runs because you explicitly told your own machine to run it. There's no network boundary to secure because there's no network involved.

A remote server has none of that. Anyone who can reach its URL can send it requests. Without authorization, "connect to this MCP server" would mean "give an unknown caller the ability to invoke your tools" — unacceptable the moment a tool does anything that costs money, exposes private data, or changes state (which is most of what makes a tool worth having).

docs.title: The shape of the flow
docs.text:
MCP's authorization spec is standard OAuth 2.1 with a few MCP-specific conventions layered on:

  1. Discovery. The client fetches a well-known metadata document from the server (/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource) to learn which authorization server issues tokens for this MCP server, and that authorization server's own metadata (/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server) to learn its endpoints.
  2. Dynamic client registration (where supported) lets the MCP client register itself with the authorization server on the fly, rather than requiring a developer to have pre-registered a client ID by hand.
  3. Authorization. The user is sent through a normal OAuth authorization code flow (with PKCE, as OAuth 2.1 requires) — log in, approve the requested scopes, get redirected back with a code.
  4. Token issuance. The client exchanges that code for an access token (and typically a refresh token).
  5. Every request after that carries the token. Authorization: Bearer <token> on each HTTP request to the MCP server.

docs.title: What this looks like from the server's side
docs.text:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
from mcp.server.auth.settings import AuthSettings

mcp = FastMCP(
    "billing-tools",
    auth=AuthSettings(
        issuer_url="https://auth.example.com",
        resource_server_url="https://mcp.example.com",
        required_scopes=["billing:read"],
    ),
)

@mcp.tool()
def list_invoices(customer_id: str) -> str:
    """Lists invoices for a customer. Requires the billing:read scope."""
    ...

The SDK handles validating the bearer token on incoming requests and rejecting ones that don't present a valid token with the required scope — your tool code only runs once that's already been checked.

docs.title: What a well-behaved client does
docs.text:
• Tries the request unauthenticated first (or reads the discovery document up front) to learn where to get a token.
  • Runs the user through the authorization flow exactly once, then reuses the resulting access token for subsequent requests, refreshing it silently when it expires.
  • Never stores the token anywhere a malicious page or process could read it more easily than it reads the user's other credentials.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. Bearer tokens, not API keys hardcoded in config. An API key baked into a config file is a long-lived, broad credential. A short-lived OAuth access token scoped to specific permissions is strictly safer: it expires, it can be scoped narrowly (billing:read but not billing:write), and it can be revoked without rotating a secret everyone shares.
  2. PKCE closes the authorization-code-interception hole. OAuth 2.1 requires PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) on every authorization code flow — the client generates a secret verifier up front, sends only a hash of it with the authorization request, and must present the original verifier when exchanging the code for a token. Even if the code is intercepted in transit, it's useless without the verifier.
  3. Discovery means no hardcoded endpoints. Because the client reads /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource and the authorization server's own metadata document, an MCP client can authenticate against any compliant server without the client's author having to pre-configure that specific server's OAuth details.
  4. Resource-scoped tokens prevent token reuse across servers. OAuth 2.1 ties a token to the specific resource server (MCP server) it was issued for, so a token stolen from one MCP server's traffic can't be replayed against a different one.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Without writing the full OAuth flow by hand (that's a lot of moving parts for an exercise), sketch out — as comments or a short markdown note next to your billing-tools server from this lesson — exactly which HTTP requests would need to happen, in order, for a brand-new client to go from "has never talked to this server before" to "successfully calling list_invoices with a valid bearer token." Use the five numbered steps above as your checklist and fill in what each one's actual HTTP method/URL would look like.

docs.title: 04 · Resource Templates & Dynamic URIs
docs.text: In Level 1, every resource had a fixed URI — config://settings, notes://all. That's fine for things that genuinely are singular. It falls apart the moment you want to expose one resource per item in a collection that could have thousands of entries. You don't want to hand-register a thousand @mcp.resource() functions. You want one handler that serves notes://{note_id} for any note_id.

docs.title: Registering a templated resource
docs.text:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("notes-templated")

notes = {
    1: "Buy milk",
    2: "Finish MCP lesson",
    3: "Call the dentist",
}

@mcp.resource("notes://{note_id}")
def get_note(note_id: str) -> str:
    """Returns a single note by id."""
    note = notes.get(int(note_id))
    if note is None:
        raise ValueError(f"No note with id {note_id}")
    return note

The {note_id} segment is a URI template variable — RFC 6570 syntax, the same templating style used in a lot of REST API tooling. When a client reads notes://7, the SDK matches it against the registered template, extracts note_id = "7", and calls get_note(note_id="7").

docs.title: Multiple variables
docs.text:
Templates aren't limited to one variable:

@mcp.resource("notes://{year}/{month}/{note_id}")
def get_dated_note(year: str, month: str, note_id: str) -> str:
    """Returns a note filed under a specific year/month."""
    ...

A client reading notes://2026/11/7 gets year="2026", month="11", note_id="7" passed to the handler.

docs.title: Discoverability: how does a client know what to fill in?
docs.text:
A plain fixed-URI resource shows up directly in resources/list. A templated resource can't — there's no finite list of every possible note_id. Instead it appears as a resource template, returned from resources/templates/list, describing the pattern itself (notes://{note_id}) plus a human-readable name and description. A client (or the model behind it) reads that template, works out a concrete note_id it's interested in — usually because a tool call just told it one exists — and then reads the fully-resolved URI.

This is why templated resources almost always appear alongside a tool that can enumerate the valid ids:

@mcp.tool()
def list_note_ids() -> list[int]:
    """Returns every valid note id, for use with the notes://{note_id} resource."""
    return list(notes.keys())

Now the model has a path: call list_note_ids, see [1, 2, 3], then read notes://2 to get that specific note's content.

Then add list_note_ids as shown above and verify, using the Inspector, that you can go from calling the tool, to reading a templated resource for one of the returned ids, to reading an id that doesn't exist and seeing your error message instead of a crash.

docs.title: 05 · Sampling: Letting a Server Ask the LLM for Completions
docs.text: Every primitive so far flows one way: the client (on the model's behalf) calls a tool, reads a resource, or fetches a prompt from the server. Sampling is the one primitive that flows the other way — a server, in the middle of handling something, asks the client's LLM to generate text for it.

docs.title: Why a server would ever want this
docs.text:
Imagine a tool that fetches a long web page and is supposed to return a short summary. Two ways to build that:

  • The server calls out to its own LLM API, using its own API key, to generate the summary.
  • The server asks the client's LLM — the same model the user is already talking to — to generate the summary, via sampling/createMessage.

The second option means the server never needs its own model access, its own API key, or its own usage bill. It borrows the model the user already has, under the user's own approval.

docs.title: Requesting a completion from a tool handler
docs.text:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
from mcp.server.fastmcp.server import Context

mcp = FastMCP("summarizer")

@mcp.tool()
async def summarize_url(url: str, ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Fetches a URL and returns a short summary of its content."""
    page_text = fetch_page_text(url)  # your own HTTP fetch, omitted here

    result = await ctx.session.create_message(
        messages=[
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": f"Summarize this in two sentences:\n\n{page_text[:4000]}",
                },
            }
        ],
        max_tokens=200,
    )
    return result.content.text

The Context object gives a tool handler access to ctx.session, which is the live connection back to the client — create_message sends a sampling/createMessage request over that connection and awaits the client's response.

docs.title: The approval step clients are expected to apply
docs.text:
A server asking to generate text on the user's model isn't free to do silently — it still costs tokens and it's still the user's model being used on the server's behalf. A well-behaved client:

  • Shows the user (or at minimum logs, for an automated client) that a server is requesting a completion, including the proposed prompt.
  • Lets the user approve, deny, or edit the request before it's sent to the model — exactly the same "human in the loop" expectation MCP applies to tool calls that do something consequential.
  • Can apply its own model/size preferences — the server can suggest hints (e.g. "a fast, cheap model is fine for this"), but the client decides which model actually serves the request.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
1. It's still just JSON-RPC, running in the opposite direction. A sampling/createMessage request is sent by the server over the same connection a tools/call request travels — the server is just the one initiating this particular request instead of responding to one.
  2. The client, not the server, decides which model answers. The server's request carries model preferences as hints (cost/speed/ intelligence priorities), not a hard model selection. This is a deliberate design choice: it keeps model access, and therefore cost and capability, entirely under the user's and client's control.
  3. This is why MCP servers generally don't need LLM API keys of their own. A server that only ever needs text generation as a sub-step of a tool can lean entirely on sampling instead of integrating a separate model provider — one less credential to manage, one less bill to pay.
  4. It composes with tool calls naturally. From the model's point of view, calling summarize_url just returns a summary — it has no idea (and doesn't need to know) that the server itself asked another model invocation to produce that summary along the way.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Modify summarize_url so the sampling request explicitly asks for a one-sentence summary instead of two, and add a style: str parameter to the tool (e.g. "neutral", "casual") that gets folded into the prompt sent via create_message. Call the tool twice with different style values through the Inspector and confirm the returned summaries actually differ in tone.

docs.title: 06 · Structured Output & Tool Input Schemas
docs.text: Level 1 let type hints generate a tool's schema automatically. That's fine for add(a: int, b: int). Real tools need real constraints — a status that can only be one of three values, a nested object, a field that's optional with a default. This lesson goes under the hood of what that schema actually is, and how to shape it on purpose.

docs.title: What a tool's schema actually looks like
docs.text:
Every tool's inputSchema is plain JSON Schema. This is what FastMCP generates for:

from typing import Literal

@mcp.tool()
def create_ticket(
    title: str,
    priority: Literal["low", "medium", "high"],
    assignee: str | None = None,
) -> str:
    """Creates a support ticket."""
    ...

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "title": { "type": "string" },
    "priority": { "type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high"] },
    "assignee": { "type": ["string", "null"] }
  },
  "required": ["title", "priority"]
}

This schema is what the model actually sees when deciding how to call the tool. A tight schema — the enum on priority especially — makes it far less likely the model ever sends "priority": "urgent" by mistake, because "urgent" was never a valid option it could have picked from.

docs.title: Nested objects
docs.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Address(BaseModel):
    street: str
    city: str
    zip_code: str

@mcp.tool()
def ship_order(order_id: str, address: Address) -> str:
    """Ships an order to the given address."""
    ...

A Pydantic model as a parameter type produces a nested object schema automatically — address becomes {"type": "object", "properties": { "street": ..., "city": ..., "zip_code": ... }} — and the SDK validates and parses the incoming JSON into a real Address instance before your handler ever runs.

docs.title: Structured tool output
docs.text:
A tool doesn't have to return only free text. Returning a Pydantic model (or a dict) lets the SDK attach a matching output schema and send back structured content a client can parse programmatically, in addition to a text fallback for the model to read directly:

class TicketResult(BaseModel):
    ticket_id: str
    status: str

@mcp.tool()
def create_ticket(title: str, priority: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]) -> TicketResult:
    """Creates a support ticket and returns its id and status."""
    ticket_id = f"T-{next_id()}"
    return TicketResult(ticket_id=ticket_id, status="open")

A client that wants to chain this ticket id into another tool call can read it directly from the structured result instead of parsing it back out of prose text.

docs.title: Validation errors the model can act on
docs.text:
When a call doesn't match the schema, don't let your handler raise a bare exception with a Python stack trace — return (or raise, through the SDK's own error path) a message that tells the model specifically what was wrong:

@mcp.tool()
def create_ticket(title: str, priority: str) -> str:
    """Creates a support ticket. priority must be low, medium, or high."""
    if priority not in ("low", "medium", "high"):
        raise ValueError(
            f"priority must be one of 'low', 'medium', 'high' — got {priority!r}"
        )
    ...

A specific error like this gives the model everything it needs to retry the call correctly on its next attempt. A bare traceback doesn't.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take the ship_order tool above and add a quantity: int field with a constraint that it must be at least 1 (use Pydantic's Field(ge=1)). Call the tool through the Inspector with quantity: 0 and quantity: -5 and confirm you get a clear validation error in both cases rather than the handler silently running with an invalid quantity.

docs.title: 07 · Wrapping a Real API: GitHub as an MCP Server
docs.text: Most MCP servers you'll build at work aren't inventing new functionality — they're exposing an API that already exists, in a shape a model can call safely. GitHub's REST API is a good real target: well-documented, widely useful, and realistic about the things you actually have to handle (auth, rate limits, pagination).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
pip install "mcp[cli]" httpx
export GITHUB_TOKEN="ghp_..."   # a personal access token with repo scope

# github_server.py
import os
import httpx
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("github-tools")

GITHUB_TOKEN = os.environ["GITHUB_TOKEN"]
BASE_URL = "https://api.github.com"

def gh_headers() -> dict:
    return {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {GITHUB_TOKEN}",
        "Accept": "application/vnd.github+json",
        "X-GitHub-Api-Version": "2022-11-28",
    }

Pulling the token from an environment variable, not a hardcoded string or a tool parameter, keeps the credential out of chat context entirely — the model never sees it, and it never ends up in a conversation log.

docs.title: Listing issues
docs.text:
@mcp.tool()
async def list_issues(owner: str, repo: str, state: str = "open") -> str:
    """Lists issues for a GitHub repo. state is 'open', 'closed', or 'all'."""
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.get(
            f"{BASE_URL}/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues",
            headers=gh_headers(),
            params={"state": state, "per_page": 20},
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        issues = resp.json()

    if not issues:
        return f"No {state} issues in {owner}/{repo}."

    lines = [f"#{i['number']}: {i['title']}" for i in issues]
    return "\n".join(lines)

docs.title: Creating an issue
docs.text:
@mcp.tool()
async def create_issue(owner: str, repo: str, title: str, body: str = "") -> str:
    """Creates a new issue in a GitHub repo."""
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.post(
            f"{BASE_URL}/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues",
            headers=gh_headers(),
            json={"title": title, "body": body},
        )
        resp.raise_for_status()
        issue = resp.json()

    return f"Created issue #{issue['number']}: {issue['html_url']}"

docs.title: Handling rate limits
docs.text:
GitHub returns rate-limit information in response headers on every request — don't wait to hit a 403 to find out you're close to the limit:

async def gh_request(client: httpx.AsyncClient, method: str, url: str, **kwargs):
    resp = await client.request(method, url, headers=gh_headers(), **kwargs)
    remaining = int(resp.headers.get("x-ratelimit-remaining", "1"))
    if remaining < 5:
        reset_at = resp.headers.get("x-ratelimit-reset")
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"GitHub rate limit nearly exhausted ({remaining} left, resets at {reset_at})."
        )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp

Route both tools above through this helper instead of calling client.get/ client.post directly, and a model that tries to hammer the API in a tight loop gets a clear error — "rate limit nearly exhausted" — instead of GitHub silently throttling or blocking the underlying token.

docs.title: What makes this a good API wrapper, not just a thin proxy
docs.text:
• Tool names and descriptions describe intent (create_issue), not raw endpoints (POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues) — the model shouldn't need to know GitHub's URL structure to use this server.
  • Only expose what's actually safe to expose. This server deliberately has no delete_repo tool — not every endpoint an API offers belongs in front of a model.
  • Summarized, not raw, responses. list_issues returns a short text summary instead of dumping GitHub's full, deeply nested JSON response — that raw payload would burn a lot of the model's context for little benefit.

Test it end to end against a real (preferably disposable/test) repository through the Inspector: list issues, pick one, comment on it, then list issues again and confirm the comment count changed.

docs.title: 08 · Testing MCP Servers (Inspector & Unit Tests)
docs.text: You've been testing every server so far by poking at it manually through the Inspector. That's the right tool for exploration — it's the wrong tool for making sure create_issue still works after you refactor it next month. This lesson covers both: deeper Inspector usage, and real automated tests.

docs.title: The Inspector, beyond "click a tool and see what happens"
docs.text:
A few features worth knowing:

  • History tab — every request and response sent during the session, in order, with full JSON. This is the easiest way to see the exact wire shape of a call without writing curl by hand.
  • Notifications — a separate panel for one-way messages (progress updates, log messages) that don't fit the request/response view.
  • Direct JSON editing — for a tool with a complex input schema, you can edit the raw JSON arguments instead of filling in a generated form, which is faster for testing edge cases like missing required fields.

Treat the Inspector as your REPL for this protocol — reach for it the moment something behaves unexpectedly, before reaching for print statements.

docs.title: Unit-testing the handler, with no protocol involved
docs.text:
The fastest, most useful tests skip the protocol layer entirely and call your tool functions as plain Python:

# test_github_server.py
import pytest
from github_server import list_issues, create_issue

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_list_issues_formats_each_as_a_line(monkeypatch):
    async def fake_get(self, url, **kwargs):
        class FakeResponse:
            def raise_for_status(self): pass
            def json(self): return [
                {"number": 1, "title": "Bug A"},
                {"number": 2, "title": "Bug B"},
            ]
        return FakeResponse()

    monkeypatch.setattr("httpx.AsyncClient.get", fake_get)

    result = await list_issues(owner="acme", repo="widgets")
    assert result == "#1: Bug A\n#2: Bug B"


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_list_issues_empty_state_message(monkeypatch):
    async def fake_get(self, url, **kwargs):
        class FakeResponse:
            def raise_for_status(self): pass
            def json(self): return []
        return FakeResponse()

    monkeypatch.setattr("httpx.AsyncClient.get", fake_get)

    result = await list_issues(owner="acme", repo="widgets")
    assert "No open issues" in result

@mcp.tool()-decorated functions are still plain async def functions underneath — importing and calling them directly, with the actual network call mocked out, is ordinary pytest with no MCP machinery involved at all. This is where almost all of your test coverage should live: it's fast, doesn't need a running server, and tests the logic that actually matters.

docs.title: A thin integration test, through the real protocol
docs.text:
For the handful of things unit tests can't catch — a tool's schema doesn't match what you think it does, or the server fails to start at all — use the SDK's in-process test client instead of mocking anything:

# test_integration.py
import pytest
from mcp.shared.memory import create_connected_server_and_client_session
from github_server import mcp

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_list_issues_tool_is_registered():
    async with create_connected_server_and_client_session(mcp._mcp_server) as client:
        tools = await client.list_tools()
        names = [t.name for t in tools.tools]
        assert "list_issues" in names
        assert "create_issue" in names

This spins up a real client/server pair connected over an in-memory transport — no subprocess, no network — and exercises the actual tools/list request. It's slower than the unit tests above and should be a much smaller fraction of your suite: a handful of smoke tests confirming the server wires up correctly, not where you test business logic.

docs.title: A testing pyramid for MCP servers
docs.text:
1. Most tests: plain unit tests on handler functions, with any outside API fully mocked — fast, numerous, test actual behavior.
  2. A few integration tests using the in-process client, confirming tools are registered with the schemas you expect and the server starts cleanly.
  3. Manual Inspector sessions for exploratory testing and debugging, not as a substitute for either of the above.

Then write one more test confirming that if the mocked response's raise_for_status() raises (simulating a 422 from GitHub, e.g. an empty title), the exception propagates out of create_issue rather than being silently swallowed.

docs.title: 09 · Deploying a Remote MCP Server
docs.text: A Streamable HTTP MCP server is, underneath the protocol, just an HTTP service. Deploying it looks almost exactly like deploying any other backend — container it, put TLS in front of it, configure it with environment variables, give it a health check.

docs.title: A Dockerfile
docs.text:
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

ENV PORT=8000
EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["python", "http_server.py"]

# requirements.txt
mcp[cli]
httpx

Make sure http_server.py reads the port from the environment instead of hardcoding it, so the same image works regardless of what port the hosting platform assigns:

import os
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("github-tools")
# ... tools from Lesson 7 ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", port=int(os.environ.get("PORT", 8000)))

docker build -t github-mcp-server .
docker run -p 8000:8000 -e GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_xxx github-mcp-server

docs.title: TLS and a reverse proxy
docs.text:
Don't terminate TLS inside the Python process. Put a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, or your cloud provider's load balancer) in front of the container, handling HTTPS termination and forwarding plain HTTP to the container on its internal port:

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name mcp.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/mcp.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/mcp.example.com/privkey.pem;

    location /mcp {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_buffering off;  # required for SSE streaming to pass through
    }
}

proxy_buffering off matters specifically because of the SSE stream from Lesson 2 — a buffering proxy will hold onto server-sent events instead of forwarding them immediately, breaking anything that depends on timely delivery.

docs.title: A health check endpoint
docs.text:
Hosting platforms and load balancers need something to poll that doesn't require a full MCP session:

from starlette.responses import PlainTextResponse

@mcp.custom_route("/healthz", methods=["GET"])
async def healthz(request):
    return PlainTextResponse("ok")

Point your platform's health check (or the load balancer's) at /healthz, not at /mcp — the MCP endpoint expects real protocol traffic, not a bare GET with no session.

docs.title: A basic production checklist
docs.text:
• Environment-variable configuration for every secret (API tokens, auth issuer URLs) — never baked into the image.
  • Structured logging to stderr or a logging service, never to stdout — the stdout-corruption rule from Level 1 only applies to stdio transport, but it's a cheap habit to keep everywhere so the same server code works on either transport without a silent trap.
  • A health check endpoint, as above, so the platform can tell a crashed container from a healthy one.
  • Graceful shutdown — handle SIGTERM by finishing in-flight requests before exiting, so a deploy or scale-down doesn't cut off an active tool call mid-response.
  • Rate limiting at the proxy layer, in addition to anything your own code does (like Lesson 7's GitHub rate-limit check), as a backstop against a misbehaving or malicious client hammering the endpoint directly.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add SIGTERM handling to http_server.py: on receiving the signal, log "shutting down" to stderr, stop accepting new connections, and exit cleanly once any in-flight request finishes (or after a 10-second timeout, whichever comes first). Test it by starting the server, sending a SIGTERM with docker stop, and confirming your log line appears before the container actually exits.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A GitHub Issues MCP Server
docs.text: This project pulls together everything from this level: a server reachable over the network, protected by authentication, wrapping a real external API, with tests and a deployable container. By the end you'll have a GitHub Issues server someone else could actually point a client at.

docs.title: Spec
docs.text:
Build a Streamable HTTP MCP server, github_issues_server.py, exposing:

Tools

  • list_issues(owner: str, repo: str, state: Literal["open", "closed", "all"] = "open") -> str — a one-line-per-issue summary, same shape as Lesson 7.
  • create_issue(owner: str, repo: str, title: str, body: str = "") -> IssueResult — returns a structured result (use Lesson 6's structured-output pattern): a Pydantic model with number: int and url: str.
  • comment_on_issue(owner: str, repo: str, issue_number: int, body: str) -> str — posts a comment, returns a confirmation with the comment's URL.

Resources

  • issue://{owner}/{repo}/{issue_number} — a templated resource (Lesson 4's pattern, with three URI variables instead of one) returning the full issue body and metadata as text.

Auth

  • The server requires a bearer token on every request (Lesson 3's pattern). For this project, a simplified scheme is acceptable: validate the incoming Authorization: Bearer <token> header against a single expected value read from an environment variable (MCP_SERVER_TOKEN), rather than standing up a full OAuth authorization server — note in a comment that a real production deployment would use the full OAuth 2.1 flow from Lesson 3, and explain in one sentence why this simplified version is acceptable for a project but not for a real multi-user deployment.

Deployment

  • A Dockerfile that builds and runs the server, reading PORT, GITHUB_TOKEN, and MCP_SERVER_TOKEN from the environment.
  • A /healthz endpoint per Lesson 9.

Tests

  • At least 4 unit tests covering list_issues, create_issue, and comment_on_issue, with the GitHub API calls mocked (Lesson 8's pattern) — including at least one test for an error path (GitHub returning a 4xx).
