docs.title: 01 · MCP vs. Function Calling vs. LangChain Tools
docs.text: If you've used an LLM API's "function calling" or "tool use" feature before, MCP can look redundant at first glance — doesn't the model already know how to call tools? The confusion is understandable, but the two sit at different layers, and a popular framework abstraction sits at a third. This lesson draws the lines precisely.

docs.title: Function calling: a model-API-level feature
docs.text:
Function/tool calling is a capability of the model's own API. You send the model a list of tool definitions (name, description, JSON Schema for arguments) alongside your prompt. The model, instead of just emitting text, can emit a structured request to call one of those tools:

{
  "type": "tool_use",
  "name": "get_weather",
  "input": {"city": "Austin"}
}

Your application code is entirely responsible for: supplying that tool list, noticing the model asked for a tool call, actually running the corresponding function, and feeding the result back into the conversation so the model can continue. The model API has no idea where get_weather's implementation lives, how it's authenticated, or whether it's even safe to run. That's 100% on you, and it's the same amount of "on you" whether you have one tool or a hundred.

docs.title: MCP: a protocol for exposing and discovering those tools
docs.text:
MCP doesn't replace function calling — it standardizes the other side of the equation: how an application discovers what tools exist, what they do, how to call them, and how to get data and reusable prompts from external systems, all through one consistent protocol instead of bespoke code per integration.

A host application (say, an IDE assistant) connects to one or more MCP servers, asks each one "what tools do you have?" via tools/list, and gets back exactly the kind of tool definitions a model's function-calling API wants: name, description, JSON Schema. The host then hands those definitions to the model as part of its normal function-calling flow. When the model asks to call one, the host routes that call to the right MCP server via tools/call, gets the result back over the protocol, and feeds it to the model — using the exact same function-calling mechanism it always has.

MCP is the plumbing that fills the tool list and executes the calls. Function calling is still the thing the model API actually does.

docs.title: Where LangChain Tools fit in
docs.text:
Frameworks like LangChain define their own Tool abstraction — a Python object with a name, description, and a callable — used to build agents within that framework. A LangChain Tool isn't a competing protocol; it's a framework-internal interface. The practical relationship is:

from langchain_mcp_adapters.tools import load_mcp_tools
from mcp import ClientSession

async def build_langchain_tools(session: ClientSession):
    # Connects to an MCP server, lists its tools, and wraps each one
    # as a LangChain Tool the framework's agent loop can call directly.
    tools = await load_mcp_tools(session)
    return tools

An adapter like this connects to an MCP server, calls tools/list, and wraps each MCP tool as a LangChain Tool whose underlying implementation calls tools/call on the MCP session. LangChain gets to keep its own agent abstractions; MCP gets to be the thing that actually talks to the external system. The same pattern repeats across other frameworks (LlamaIndex, AutoGen, and others each ship or support similar MCP adapters) — MCP servers become a portable backend any of them can plug into, instead of writing a GitHub integration once per framework.

docs.title: When each is the right choice
docs.text:
• Just need the model to call a couple of functions you already wrote, in one app, with no reuse goal? Plain function calling is simpler — don't reach for MCP just because it exists.
  • Building or using a tool/data integration you want any MCP-compatible host to be able to use (your own app today, a different app tomorrow, someone else's app ever) — that's exactly what MCP is for.
  • Already committed to a framework like LangChain for agent orchestration, but want your tools to also work outside that framework? Build an MCP server, then use the framework's MCP adapter to pull those tools in. You get framework-native usage and portability at the same time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The path from "you wrote an MCP tool" to "the model actually calls it" runs through several translations, not one:

  1. Your server defines a tool. With the Python SDK's @mcp.tool() decorator, your function's type hints and docstring become a JSON Schema tool definition the server can report.
  2. The host asks for the list. On connecting, the host's MCP client sends tools/list; the server responds with every registered tool's name, description, and inputSchema (plain JSON Schema).
  3. The host reshapes that into the model API's format. Every model provider has its own expected tool-definition shape even though most are JSON-Schema-based — field names and wrapping differ slightly between, say, Claude's API and another provider's. The host (or an SDK's model adapter layer) does this reshaping; MCP's inputSchema is the common source of truth it reshapes from.
  4. The model emits a call in its own API's native format — it never sees MCP at all, only the function-calling format it was given.
  5. The host maps the call back to MCP. It matches the model's tool-call name back to the originating server and sends a tools/call request with the model-supplied arguments.
  6. The result comes back over MCP, then gets reshaped again into whatever "tool result" format the model API expects, and the model continues the conversation.

MCP never talks to the model directly. It's the standardized layer the host sits between to avoid writing that discovery-and-execution plumbing once per integration per model provider.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick any two tools from a server you built in an earlier level (or write two small ones now). Write out, by hand, what each tool's inputSchema looks like as returned by tools/list. Then write a short paragraph for each tool describing in plain English what you'd expect a host to need to change to present that same schema to a specific model API of your choice (you don't need real API docs open — reason about what a model-facing function definition typically needs: a name, a description, and the parameters). This is the translation step from "How It Actually Works" — the point is to see concretely that MCP's schema and the model's function-calling schema are related but not identical formats.

docs.title: 02 · Building a Custom Transport
docs.text: Every MCP message — a tool call, a resource read, a progress notification — is the same JSON-RPC 2.0 payload no matter how it physically travels between client and server. stdio and Streamable HTTP are the two transports the spec and official SDKs ship out of the box, but the protocol layer above them doesn't actually care how bytes move. This lesson builds a third one.

docs.title: Why you'd need a custom transport
docs.text:
The built-in transports cover the overwhelming majority of real use cases — local subprocess (stdio) and remote HTTP (Streamable HTTP). You'd reach for a custom transport mainly when:

  • You're embedding an MCP client in a browser, where raw TCP and subprocess spawning aren't available, but a WebSocket is.
  • You need to carry MCP messages over an existing messaging system your infrastructure already uses (an internal message bus, for instance), and bridging through HTTP would be an unnecessary extra hop.
  • You're prototyping transport-level behavior the spec doesn't define yet and want to experiment before proposing it upstream.

docs.title: The transport interface
docs.text:
Both SDKs define a transport as something that can send and receive JSON-RPC messages asynchronously — in the Python SDK, concretely, a transport is responsible for producing a pair of async read/write streams that the protocol layer reads messages from and writes messages to. A custom transport's job is just to implement that pairing over whatever underlying channel you're using.

import asyncio
import json
import websockets
from mcp.shared.message import SessionMessage
from mcp.types import JSONRPCMessage

async def websocket_client_streams(uri: str):
    """Open a WebSocket and expose it as the (read_stream, write_stream)
    pair the MCP ClientSession expects."""
    ws = await websockets.connect(uri)

    read_queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue()
    write_queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue()

    async def pump_incoming():
        async for raw in ws:
            message = JSONRPCMessage.model_validate_json(raw)
            await read_queue.put(SessionMessage(message))

    async def pump_outgoing():
        while True:
            session_message = await write_queue.get()
            raw = session_message.message.model_dump_json(exclude_none=True)
            await ws.send(raw)

    asyncio.create_task(pump_incoming())
    asyncio.create_task(pump_outgoing())
    return read_queue, write_queue

This is a sketch, not a drop-in SDK class — the exact stream types and session wiring are worth checking against the SDK version you're using, since the low-level transport interface is one of the more actively evolving corners of the SDKs. The shape that matters conceptually: one coroutine pumping inbound frames into a queue the session reads from, one pumping outbound messages the session writes onto the wire.

docs.title: Server-side: the mirror image
docs.text:
A WebSocket server transport does the same job in reverse — accept a connection, decode each incoming frame as a JSONRPCMessage, hand it to the server's message-handling loop, and encode outgoing messages (responses, notifications) back onto the socket:

import websockets
from mcp.server.lowlevel import Server
from mcp.types import JSONRPCMessage

async def handle_connection(websocket, mcp_server: Server):
    async def read_stream():
        async for raw in websocket:
            yield JSONRPCMessage.model_validate_json(raw)

    async def write_message(message: JSONRPCMessage):
        await websocket.send(message.model_dump_json(exclude_none=True))

    await mcp_server.run(read_stream(), write_message, mcp_server.create_initialization_options())

Everything your server already registered — tools, resources, prompts — works unchanged. Only the bytes-in, bytes-out mechanism is new.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A transport implementation has exactly one contract to honor, regardless of language or SDK version:

  1. Preserve message boundaries. Each JSON-RPC message must arrive at the other end as a complete, independent unit — WebSocket frames and newline-delimited stdio both give you this for free; a raw TCP stream would not, and you'd need your own framing (length-prefixing, for example).
  2. Preserve ordering per direction, but don't assume request/response pairs are strictly interleaved — notifications and requests for different in-flight calls can be mixed on the wire, and the id field is what lets the session layer match a response back to its request, not arrival order.
  3. Be bidirectional and duplex-capable. A server can send the client requests too (an elicitation request or a sampling/createMessage call, for instance), so a transport that only supports client-to-server messages — some naive HTTP polling designs — isn't sufficient for a fully capable connection.
  4. Surface connection lifecycle events (closed, errored) so the session layer above can clean up and the host can decide whether to reconnect.
  5. Everything above this layer — initialization, capability negotiation, tool calls — is written against the abstract read/write stream interface, not against stdio or HTTP specifically. That's precisely why a correctly implemented custom transport is a drop-in swap: no other part of your server or client code changes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Using the WebSocket sketches above as a starting point, get a minimal round trip working: a WebSocket server transport wrapping a FastMCP server with one trivial tool, and a WebSocket client transport that connects, calls initialize, lists tools, and calls the one tool. You don't need TLS or auth for this exercise — just prove the message pump in both directions actually carries a real tool call end to end.

docs.title: 03 · MCP for RAG: Servers as a Retrieval Layer
docs.text: Retrieval-augmented generation systems need a way to turn a query into relevant chunks of content, usually by searching a vector database. Nothing about that requires MCP — you can call your vector database's client library directly from inside your application. This lesson is about when putting an MCP server in front of that retrieval step is worth the extra layer, and when it isn't.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
Instead of your application importing a vector-database client and querying it in-process, you stand up an MCP server whose tool or resource does that querying on the application's behalf:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import chromadb

mcp = FastMCP("knowledge-base")
client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_data")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection("docs")

@mcp.tool()
def search_knowledge_base(query: str, top_k: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
    """Search the knowledge base for chunks relevant to a query.

    Returns a list of {text, source, score} for the top_k most similar
    chunks.
    """
    results = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=top_k)
    return [
        {"text": doc, "source": meta.get("source"), "score": dist}
        for doc, meta, dist in zip(
            results["documents"][0],
            results["metadatas"][0],
            results["distances"][0],
        )
    ]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

If you've worked through the Vector Databases Mastery Path series on this same site, everything inside that tool body — the embedding, the similarity search, the index choice — is exactly what that course covers in depth. This lesson is only about the layer around that: should it live behind an MCP server at all?

docs.title: The tradeoff, honestly
docs.text:
What you gain:

  • Reusability across hosts. Any MCP-compatible application — your internal chat tool today, a different IDE assistant tomorrow, a teammate's side project next month — gets the same retrieval tool for free, with no re-integration.
  • Discoverability. tools/list tells a host (and the model) exactly what this tool does and what arguments it takes, without anyone reading your application's source code.
  • A clean security boundary. The server process is the only thing that needs direct credentials/network access to the vector database; client applications never touch it directly.

What it costs:

  • An extra network hop and serialization step, even for a local stdio server — meaningful if you're doing many small retrieval calls in a tight loop and latency is the dominant constraint.
  • Another process to deploy, monitor, and keep in sync with your vector database's schema and embedding model version.
  • Indirection that can genuinely not be worth it for a single application that will only ever call its own retrieval logic — if nothing else will ever need this tool, in-process is simpler and faster, full stop.

docs.title: When it's worth it
docs.text: Reach for an MCP retrieval server when the knowledge base is a shared asset multiple tools or applications should be able to query, when you want the retrieval step to be independently deployable and scalable from the application calling it, or when you specifically want a model to be able to decide when to search (as an available tool) rather than always retrieving on every turn — the tool-call framing gives the model that choice instead of hard-coding "always retrieve first."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take a retrieval function you'd otherwise call directly in an application (or write a small one against any local dataset) and wrap it as an MCP tool the way the example above does. Then write two or three sentences arguing honestly for your specific use case: is the MCP-server layer actually worth it here, or would direct in-process integration genuinely be the better call? There's no "right" answer expected — the point is practicing making that tradeoff call deliberately instead of reaching for MCP by default.

docs.title: 04 · Multi-Agent Systems Built on MCP
docs.text: It's tempting to reach for MCP as the answer to "how do my agents talk to each other," but that's not what the protocol is for. This lesson is deliberately about drawing that line clearly, then showing the pattern that actually does work well: multiple agents, each with their own MCP client, sharing a common set of MCP servers.

docs.title: What MCP is not: an agent-to-agent protocol
docs.text: MCP connects a host application (which may itself be a single agent) to servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts. There is no concept in the spec of one agent sending a message to another agent as a peer — the client/server relationship is inherently between an application and its tool/data providers, not between two equally-capable agents negotiating a task. If you need agent-to-agent coordination, that's a separate concern your system needs to solve on top of (or alongside) MCP, not something MCP hands you.

docs.title: What does work: shared servers, independent clients
docs.text:
The pattern that holds up in practice is each agent running its own MCP client(s), independently connecting to the same servers your organization already runs:

 Agent A (research)         Agent B (writer)         Agent C (reviewer)
      │  client                   │  client                 │  client
      ▼                           ▼                         ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │        Shared MCP servers: search, docs, file storage        │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Each agent connects, lists tools, and calls them independently — there's no MCP-level awareness that other agents exist. The servers don't know or care how many clients are connected; each connection is just another client as far as the protocol is concerned. This gives you real benefits without inventing a new protocol:

  • One place to maintain the integration (a search tool, a docs tool) no matter how many agents end up using it.
  • Consistent permissions and auditing, since every agent's tool calls go through the same server-side logic, logging, and access control.
  • Agents can be added or removed freely without touching the servers at all.

docs.title: Where actual coordination happens
docs.text:
If agent A's output needs to become agent B's input, or agent C needs to know what A and B already did, that's orchestration logic your application owns — a shared state store, a message queue, a workflow engine, or simply one orchestrating process that calls each agent in sequence and passes results along. A simple, concrete version: a coordinator process holds a blackboard a task's results get written to, with each agent reading what it needs from that blackboard before starting its own MCP-backed work, and writing its results back when done. MCP is in this picture only as what each agent uses to reach the outside world — the coordination itself happens entirely outside the protocol.

# a minimal coordinator — NOT part of MCP, just application logic
blackboard = {}

async def run_research_agent(session):
    results = await session.call_tool("search_web", {"query": "..."})
    blackboard["research"] = results

async def run_writer_agent(session):
    draft = await generate_draft(blackboard["research"])
    blackboard["draft"] = draft
    await session.call_tool("save_file", {"path": "draft.md", "content": draft})

docs.title: A note on emerging agent-to-agent protocols
docs.text: Separate efforts exist in the wider ecosystem specifically aimed at agent-to-agent communication — letting one agent discover and delegate work to another agent as a peer, rather than to a tool. Those are a genuinely different layer of the stack from MCP, and the two are complementary rather than competing: an agent exposed via an agent-to-agent protocol might internally use MCP to reach its own tools and data, the same way any other MCP host would.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Sketch (in code or in a short diagram-in-prose) a two-agent system where both agents connect independently to one shared MCP server exposing a search_docs tool. Write the minimal coordinator logic that runs agent A first, passes its result to agent B, and have agent B call the same shared tool with a query derived from A's output. The point is to see, concretely, that the "coordination" part is ordinary application code sitting entirely outside of MCP.

docs.title: 05 · An Internal MCP Server Registry/Gateway
docs.text: Once an organization has more than a couple of internal MCP servers — search, a ticketing system, internal docs, a deploy tool — making every client connect to every server individually gets unwieldy fast: N clients each independently configuring N server connections, N sets of credentials, and N places that need to agree on access policy. A gateway collapses that into one connection point.

docs.title: What a gateway actually does
docs.text:
A gateway is itself an MCP server from a client's point of view, but instead of implementing tools directly, it proxies tools/list and tools/call (and the resource/prompt equivalents) to a set of registered backend servers, aggregating their capabilities into one combined list and routing each call to the right backend.

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client, StdioServerParameters

mcp = FastMCP("internal-gateway")

# registry: server name -> connection parameters
BACKENDS = {
    "search": StdioServerParameters(command="mcp-search-server"),
    "tickets": StdioServerParameters(command="mcp-tickets-server"),
}

_sessions: dict[str, ClientSession] = {}

async def get_session(backend: str) -> ClientSession:
    if backend not in _sessions:
        read, write = await stdio_client(BACKENDS[backend]).__aenter__()
        session = ClientSession(read, write)
        await session.initialize()
        _sessions[backend] = session
    return _sessions[backend]

@mcp.tool()
async def search_search_docs(query: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Proxy to the 'search' backend's search_docs tool."""
    session = await get_session("search")
    result = await session.call_tool("search_docs", {"query": query})
    return result.content

A production gateway generalizes this: instead of hand-writing one proxy tool per backend tool, it calls tools/list on each backend at startup (or on a refresh interval), namespaces each tool by backend (search.search_docs, tickets.create_ticket — tying back to the namespacing pattern from Level 3), and dynamically registers a proxying handler for each one.

docs.title: Where auth and policy belong
docs.text:
The gateway is the single place every call passes through, which makes it the natural enforcement point for things that would otherwise need duplicating in every backend server:

  • Authenticating the calling client once, at the gateway, instead of each backend server independently validating credentials.
  • Per-client, per-tool authorization — a service account for an internal chatbot might be allowed search.* but not tickets.create_ticket, enforced centrally before a call is ever forwarded.
  • Consistent audit logging of every tool call across every backend, in one place, in one format — the natural home for the observability patterns from Level 3.
  • Rate limiting and caching applied uniformly, rather than reimplemented per backend.
ALLOWED_TOOLS = {
    "chatbot-service": {"search.search_docs"},
    "ops-dashboard": {"search.search_docs", "tickets.create_ticket"},
}

async def authorize(client_id: str, tool_name: str):
    if tool_name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS.get(client_id, set()):
        raise PermissionError(f"{client_id} is not authorized for {tool_name}")

docs.title: The registry half
docs.text: The "registry" piece is simply the gateway's backend list made discoverable and manageable on its own — a config file, a small database table, or an admin API that lets backends register themselves (and deregister on shutdown) rather than being hard-coded. At small scale a static config file is entirely sufficient; dynamic registration only earns its complexity once backends are added and removed often enough that editing a config file by hand becomes the actual bottleneck.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Extend the sketch above into a working gateway with two backend servers of your own (reuse ones from earlier levels, or stub two trivial ones). Add the namespacing step so tool names are prefixed by backend automatically instead of hand-written per tool, and add the simple authorize() check shown above gating at least one tool behind a specific client identity.

docs.title: 06 · Versioning & Backward Compatibility
docs.text: Two different kinds of "versioning" matter in an MCP system, and they're easy to conflate: the version of the MCP protocol itself, negotiated on every connection, and the version of your server's own tool set, which evolves on your own schedule. This lesson covers both.

docs.title: Protocol version negotiation
docs.text:
Every connection starts with the client sending an initialize request that includes the protocol version it supports:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "initialize",
  "params": {
    "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18",
    "capabilities": {},
    "clientInfo": {"name": "example-host", "version": "1.0.0"}
  }
}

The server responds with the protocol version it will use for this session — either the client's requested version if it supports it, or a different version it does support, along with its own capabilities:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "result": {
    "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18",
    "capabilities": {"tools": {}, "resources": {"subscribe": true}},
    "serverInfo": {"name": "docs-server", "version": "2.1.0"}
  }
}

If the client doesn't support the version the server comes back with, it's expected to close the connection rather than proceed on a protocol version it can't correctly implement. This exchange happens exactly once, before initialized is sent and normal operation begins — there's no mid-session protocol version switching.

docs.title: Capabilities: declaring what you actually support
docs.text: Alongside the protocol version, both sides declare capabilities — which optional parts of the spec they implement. A server that doesn't support resource subscriptions simply omits subscribe: true from its capabilities.resources object; a client should check for a capability before relying on it rather than assuming every server supports everything the spec defines. This is the main lever that lets the protocol add new optional features over time without breaking servers and clients that predate them.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The negotiation is designed around a specific failure mode: a client and server built against different protocol-spec dates connecting to each other.

  1. The client proposes a version it was built against. This is the version whose request/response shapes its SDK code actually implements.
  2. The server either confirms that version or proposes an alternative it does support. A well-behaved server should support at least one version the client is likely to understand; SDKs typically track a small range of recent spec versions rather than only the very latest.
  3. The client must validate the server's answer, not just assume success — proceeding with a protocol version your client code doesn't actually implement is how you get obscure runtime errors on the first real request rather than a clean failure at startup.
  4. Capabilities are the finer-grained compatibility signal within a given protocol version — two implementations can agree on the same protocol version and still differ on which optional features they support, which is exactly why capabilities are negotiated separately rather than implied by version number alone.

docs.title: Evolving your own tool set without breaking clients
docs.text:
Separately from protocol versioning, your server's tools, resources, and prompts change over time as you add features. The practical rules that keep existing clients working:

  • Adding a new tool is always safe — clients that don't know about it simply never call it.
  • Adding a new optional parameter to an existing tool is safe, as long as it has a sensible default and omitting it preserves the old behavior.
  • Removing a tool, renaming a tool, or changing a required parameter's type is a breaking change — treat it exactly like a breaking API change anywhere else: version your server's own release (your serverInfo.version field, and ideally your own changelog), give existing integrations notice, and consider keeping the old tool as a deprecated alias for a transition period rather than deleting it outright.
  • Changing what a tool's description promises, even without changing its schema, is also a real compatibility break from the model's point of view — a model relying on the old description to decide when to call the tool may now call it at the wrong moments.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take a tool from any server you built in an earlier level. Write two versions of its definition: the current one, and a "v2" that adds one new optional parameter with a safe default. Confirm (by reasoning through it, or by actually testing with an old client call that doesn't pass the new parameter) that the old call still behaves identically under the new version — that's the concrete bar "backward compatible" needs to clear.

docs.title: 07 · Scaling MCP Servers in Production
docs.text: Scaling an MCP server mostly means scaling an ordinary web service — until you hit the one place MCP is genuinely different from a typical REST API: long-lived, server-initiated streaming connections. This lesson covers both halves.

docs.title: Stateless servers: the easy case
docs.text:
A server that keeps no in-memory session state between requests — every tools/call is handled using only the arguments in that request, with anything persistent (user data, cached results) living in an external store like a database or cache — scales exactly like any stateless HTTP service:

            ┌──────────────┐
  clients → │ Load Balancer │ → server instance 1
            └──────────────┘ → server instance 2
                             → server instance 3

Any instance can handle any request. Add instances under load, remove them when load drops, and a standard load balancer with a basic health check is all the routing logic you need. If your server's tools only ever read from or write to external systems (a database, an API) rather than holding state in the process itself, aim to keep it stateless — it's by far the simpler scaling story.

docs.title: Stateful servers: the real constraint
docs.text:
A server using the Streamable HTTP transport's SSE stream for server-initiated messages (progress notifications, sampling requests) has a connection a specific client is actively listening on. If a load balancer routes that client's next request to a different instance than the one holding its open stream, the server-initiated messages have nowhere to go.

            ┌──────────────┐
  client  → │ Load Balancer │ → instance A  ← client's SSE stream is HERE
                             → instance B  ← a later request lands here
                                               and can't reach the stream

The standard fixes, in order of how much they cost you:

  • Session affinity (sticky sessions) at the load balancer — route a given Mcp-Session-Id to the same backend instance for the life of the session. Simple to configure, but it means that instance's failure drops every session pinned to it, and it can produce uneven load if some sessions are much longer-lived than others.
  • A shared pub/sub backbone between instances (Redis Streams, a message queue) — any instance can receive a request, and if the client's session is pinned to a different instance's stream, the receiving instance publishes the message for the owning instance to pick up and forward. More infrastructure, but no single instance failure drops sessions it isn't directly holding.
  • Externalizing session state entirely, so "which instance owns this session" is a lookup in a shared store rather than a load-balancer routing decision baked in at connection time — the most flexible option, and the most work to build correctly.

Most teams start with sticky sessions and only move to a shared backbone once session-affinity failures or load imbalance actually become a measured problem — building the pub/sub version up front for a server that doesn't need it yet is usually wasted complexity.

docs.title: Connection pooling to backends
docs.text:
A server's tools very often call out to something else — a database, an internal API, another MCP server behind a gateway. Under concurrent load, opening a fresh connection per tool call to each of those backends adds real, avoidable latency and can exhaust the backend's own connection limits. Pool connections to each backend the same way you would in any backend service:

import asyncpg

_pool: asyncpg.Pool | None = None

async def get_db_pool() -> asyncpg.Pool:
    global _pool
    if _pool is None:
        _pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(dsn="...", min_size=2, max_size=10)
    return _pool

@mcp.tool()
async def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    pool = await get_db_pool()
    async with pool.acquire() as conn:
        row = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", user_id)
        return dict(row)

Size the pool against the backend's own connection limit divided by the number of server instances you expect to run concurrently, not against a guess — an oversized pool across many instances is a common way to accidentally exhaust a database's connection limit under scale-out.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: For a server you've already built (pick one with at least one tool that calls an external system), write a short scaling plan: is it stateless or does it rely on server-initiated SSE messages? If stateless, what would you need at the load balancer? If stateful, which of the three fixes above would you reach for first, and why? Then add connection pooling to any tool in it that currently opens a fresh connection per call.

docs.title: 08 · Enterprise Governance: Audit Logs & Compliance
docs.text: Once MCP servers sit between a model and real systems of record — customer data, financial records, infrastructure that can be changed — "it worked in testing" stops being enough. This lesson covers what an enterprise deployment needs beyond the functional correctness earlier levels focused on: who can prove what happened, and who approved it.

docs.title: What a real audit log entry needs
docs.text:
A log line that just says tool called: update_customer is close to useless for compliance purposes. A usable audit record captures, at minimum:

import time, json, uuid

def audit_log(tool_name: str, arguments: dict, caller_identity: str, result_summary: str):
    entry = {
        "event_id": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "timestamp": time.time(),
        "tool": tool_name,
        "arguments": arguments,         # redact sensitive fields before logging
        "caller": caller_identity,      # the authenticated client/user, not just "a model"
        "result_summary": result_summary,
        "outcome": "success",           # or "denied" / "error"
    }
    # write to an append-only, tamper-evident store — not a rotating
    # local file a process can quietly lose on restart
    write_to_audit_store(entry)

The non-negotiable fields: what was called, with what arguments, on whose authority (tying back to the auth work from Level 2 — the authenticated identity behind the call, not just "the AI did it"), when, and what happened. "On whose authority" matters even more in an MCP context than a typical API: the acting party is an AI system a human asked to do something, and compliance usually needs to trace the action back to that human, not stop at "the model decided to."

docs.title: Data residency and PII
docs.text:
Tools that read or write personal data carry the same obligations any other system touching that data does — MCP doesn't create new ones, but it's easy to lose track of them once a tool is just "something the model can call." Concretely:

  • Know which tools touch PII, and treat their schemas and logs accordingly — the audit log shown above should redact or hash sensitive argument fields rather than logging them in the clear.
  • Respect data residency requirements at the server level: if a regulation requires EU customer data to stay in the EU, that constrains where the server handling that tool can run and what it's allowed to call out to — not something the model or the protocol can enforce for you.
  • Apply the same retention and deletion rules to tool call history that apply to the underlying data — an audit log that retains deleted customers' PII indefinitely can itself become a compliance problem.

docs.title: Approval workflows for high-risk tools
docs.text:
Not every tool should execute the instant the model calls it. For genuinely high-risk actions (an irreversible database delete, a large financial transaction, a production deployment), insert a human approval step between the model's call and the tool's execution:

@mcp.tool()
async def delete_customer_account(customer_id: str, reason: str) -> dict:
    """Request deletion of a customer account. Requires human approval
    before this actually executes."""
    approval = await request_human_approval(
        action="delete_customer_account",
        details={"customer_id": customer_id, "reason": reason},
    )
    if not approval.approved:
        return {"status": "denied", "reason": approval.denial_reason}

    await perform_deletion(customer_id)
    return {"status": "completed"}

This is the server-side complement to the client-side per-tool consent pattern from Level 3's scopes-and-permissions lesson: that lesson was about a host asking a user "allow this tool call?" before sending it; this is about a server refusing to complete a genuinely high-risk action without its own independent approval gate, which matters even if the calling host's own consent prompt was somehow bypassed or misconfigured. Defense in depth, not a single checkpoint either side can rely on alone.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Take one tool from any server you've built that modifies state (creates, updates, or deletes something). Add: (1) an audit log call capturing the fields listed above with sensitive arguments redacted, and (2) a human approval gate modeled on the example, even if request_human_approval is just a stub that prompts on the terminal for this exercise. Confirm the tool refuses to act when approval is denied.

docs.title: 09 · Where MCP Is Headed
docs.text: Every other lesson in this course describes the spec and ecosystem as they exist today. This one is deliberately different: a snapshot of where things are trending, written with the honesty that a protocol this actively developed will keep moving. Read it as "worth watching," not "guaranteed."

docs.title: Public server registries and directories
docs.text: As the number of MCP servers in the wild has grown, so has demand for a way to discover trustworthy ones without word-of-mouth — public directories and registry efforts that index available servers, show their capabilities, and in some cases attach provenance or verification signals, are an active area of ecosystem investment. The practical implication for you: as these mature, "build it yourself" and "find a vetted existing server" are both increasingly real options for common integrations, and part of a responsible build-vs-use decision will mean checking whether a well- maintained server for what you need already exists before writing a new one.

docs.title: Elicitation maturing
docs.text: Elicitation — a primitive letting a server ask the user a question mid-task and get a direct answer back, rather than only returning results to the model and hoping the conversation surfaces what it needs — is a newer addition to the spec than tools, resources, and prompts, and tooling and SDK support for it is still catching up to those more established primitives. Where it's heading: richer structured elicitation (not just free-text prompts, but typed forms a host can render properly), and wider adoption in servers that need information the model itself doesn't have and shouldn't guess at — credentials, confirmations, disambiguating choices.

docs.title: Broader cross-vendor adoption
docs.text: MCP started as an Anthropic-led open standard, but the stated goal — and the visible trend — is a protocol that works the same regardless of which AI provider's model a host happens to be using. Growing support for MCP across other model providers and agent frameworks is the direction this has been moving; the practical bet worth making today is that a well-built MCP server is an investment in infrastructure that outlives any single model provider relationship, not a Claude-specific integration.

docs.title: Multi-modal resources
docs.text: Early resource content was overwhelmingly text. As agent use cases expand into images, audio, and other media, expect resource and tool result types to keep expanding to carry that content natively through the protocol rather than requiring awkward base64-in-text workarounds — some of this groundwork already exists in the spec today, with the direction being wider, more ergonomic support across SDKs.

docs.title: What to actually do with this lesson
docs.text: Don't build around any single prediction here as if it were already settled — build servers that follow the spec as it exists today, keep them loosely enough coupled to specific SDK internals that upgrading is realistic, and revisit this lesson's claims periodically against the actual, current specification rather than trusting this snapshot to stay accurate indefinitely. The most durable skill from this whole course isn't memorizing today's primitive list — it's understanding the protocol's design well enough to keep up as it evolves.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Go find the current, official MCP specification changelog or release notes (search for "Model Context Protocol specification changelog"). Pick one change from the most recent few entries and write two or three sentences on what problem it solves and whether it confirms, extends, or contradicts any of the trends described above. This lesson will age — practice checking it against the real source rather than taking it as fixed.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone Project — A Production-Grade MCP Server Suite
docs.text: This is the final project of the course. Everything from "What Is MCP & Why It Exists" through yesterday's lesson on emerging trends has been building toward this: a small but genuinely production-shaped suite of MCP servers, not a single toy example. The goal isn't to follow a tutorial to the end — it's to make the real design decisions yourself, using the vocabulary and techniques this course gave you, and end up with something you could actually point to as evidence you've mastered this material.

docs.title: What you're building
docs.text:
A gateway (Level 4, lesson 5) sitting in front of two or three backend MCP servers of your own choosing, with:

  • Authentication on the gateway using the OAuth 2.1 pattern from Level 2
  • Audit logging of every tool call, in the shape from yesterday's lesson
  • An approval gate on at least one genuinely state-changing tool
  • Tests covering both individual backend tool logic and the gateway's routing/authorization behavior
  • Observability — structured logs and request correlation, from Level 3

You get to choose what the backend servers actually do. Pick something you can build real, working tools for rather than stubs — a notes/tasks server like Level 1's project, a wrapper around a real public API like Level 2's GitHub project, a retrieval server backed by a small local dataset (Level 4, lesson 3) — any combination of two or three is fine, as long as each one has at least two real tools.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
┌───────────────────────┐
  MCP client (you,  ───► │   Gateway (FastMCP)    │
  or Inspector)          │  - OAuth-authenticated │
                         │  - namespaces tools     │
                         │  - authorizes per-tool  │
                         │  - audit-logs every call│
                         └──────────┬─────────────┘
                                    │  proxies tools/call, tools/list
                     ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                     ▼              ▼              ▼
              ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────┐
              │ Backend A │  │ Backend B │  │ Backend C │
              │ (stdio or │  │ (stdio or │  │ (optional)│
              │  HTTP)    │  │  HTTP)    │  │           │
              └───────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────┘

A client only ever talks to the gateway. The gateway is the only thing that knows how many backends exist, where they live, and who's allowed to call what on them — exactly the design from Level 4, lesson 5, now with real auth and audit logging layered on top of it.

docs.title: Required components checklist
docs.text:
Work through this as your actual build checklist, not just a reading list:

  • [ ] Two or three backend MCP servers, each with at least two real tools (not stubs that return hardcoded data)
  • [ ] A gateway that aggregates all backend tools into one tools/list response, with tool names namespaced by backend (notes.add_task, github.create_issue, etc.)
  • [ ] Routing: the gateway correctly forwards a tools/call for a namespaced tool to the right backend and returns its result unmodified
  • [ ] OAuth-based authentication on the gateway's HTTP transport — a client without a valid token is rejected before any tool call is considered
  • [ ] Per-client authorization — at least two distinct "client identities" with different allowed tool sets, enforced at the gateway (reuse or extend the authorize() pattern from lesson 5)
  • [ ] Audit logging of every tool call through the gateway: tool name, arguments (sensitive fields redacted), caller identity, timestamp, outcome — written somewhere durable, not just printed to a console that scrolls away
  • [ ] An approval gate on at least one state-changing tool, following the pattern from yesterday's lesson — calling it should visibly pause for approval, and a denial should prevent the underlying action from happening
  • [ ] Structured, correlated logging — every log line for a single end-to-end request (gateway receives call → forwards to backend → backend responds → gateway responds) should share a request ID you can grep for
  • [ ] A test suite covering: at least one backend tool's logic directly (unit-style, no protocol layer involved), and the gateway's authorization behavior (a disallowed tool call for a given identity is actually rejected, not silently allowed)
  • [ ] A README for the whole suite: what it does, how to run it, and a short "architecture decisions" section explaining the choices you made and why — the kind of document you'd actually want if you inherited this project from someone else

docs.title: Suggested build phases
docs.text:
Don't try to build all of this at once. A workable order:

  1. Backends first, standalone. Get your two or three backend servers working and manually testable with the MCP Inspector before any gateway exists. Confirm each one's tools behave correctly in isolation.
  2. Naive gateway, no auth yet. Build the proxying/namespacing gateway from lesson 5 with no authentication at all — just prove the routing works end to end: a client calls the gateway, the gateway calls the right backend, the result comes back correctly.
  3. Add authentication. Layer OAuth 2.1 on the gateway's HTTP transport. Confirm an unauthenticated call is rejected and an authenticated one still works.
  4. Add authorization, audit logging, and the approval gate together — they naturally sit in the same code path (every call passes through the gateway's dispatch logic), so building them in the same pass keeps that logic coherent rather than bolted on in three separate, possibly conflicting places.
  5. Add structured, correlated logging across the whole request path.
  6. Write the tests last, against the real behavior you've built — not speculative tests against behavior you haven't implemented yet.
  7. Write the README.

docs.title: A starting skeleton for the gateway's dispatch path
docs.text:
This is intentionally incomplete — it shows where each piece from the checklist plugs in, not a finished implementation:

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("capstone-gateway")

async def dispatch_tool_call(caller_identity: str, tool_name: str, arguments: dict):
    # 1. Authorization
    if not is_authorized(caller_identity, tool_name):
        audit_log(tool_name, arguments, caller_identity, outcome="denied")
        raise PermissionError(f"{caller_identity} is not authorized for {tool_name}")

    # 2. Approval gate (only for tools that need it)
    if requires_approval(tool_name):
        approval = await request_human_approval(tool_name, arguments)
        if not approval.approved:
            audit_log(tool_name, arguments, caller_identity, outcome="approval_denied")
            return {"status": "denied", "reason": approval.denial_reason}

    # 3. Route to the correct backend
    backend_name, real_tool_name = tool_name.split(".", 1)
    session = await get_backend_session(backend_name)
    result = await session.call_tool(real_tool_name, arguments)

    # 4. Audit the completed call
    audit_log(tool_name, arguments, caller_identity, outcome="success")
    return result

Everything this function calls — is_authorized, requires_approval, request_human_approval, get_backend_session, audit_log — is yours to design and implement, pulling directly from the earlier lessons each one corresponds to.

docs.title: Deliverable checklist (what "done" looks like)
docs.text:
• [ ] All items in the Required Components checklist are implemented and actually work, not just stubbed
  • [ ] You can start the whole suite, connect with the MCP Inspector (or a small client script) through the gateway, authenticate, and successfully call at least one tool on each backend
  • [ ] A denied authorization attempt and a denied approval request both produce a clean, logged failure rather than a crash
  • [ ] The test suite passes and actually exercises the authorization and approval logic, not just the happy path
  • [ ] The README would let someone else run and understand this project without asking you questions

This project is meant to take real, multi-day effort — treat it as evidence you can design and build production-shaped MCP infrastructure, not as a checkbox to rush through. Congratulations on reaching the end of the course.
